concepts.name: Ideological Foundations of Extremism vs. Moderatism
key_dimensions: Core philosophical differences: self-reliance vs. constitutional petitioning
Extremist critique of Moderate 'mendicancy' and 'political begging'
Role of Hindu revivalism and cultural nationalism in Extremist thought
UPSC trap: Extremists were NOT anti-constitutional per se — they sought swaraj within a framework, not anarchy

concepts.name: Bal Gangadhar Tilak: Ideology and Political Philosophy
key_dimensions: Swaraj as a birthright — origin, context, and implications of the slogan
Use of religion and culture (Ganapati/Shivaji festivals) as political mobilization tools
Tilak's interpretation of the Bhagavad Gita — 'Gita Rahasya' and the doctrine of selfless action
UPSC trap: Tilak used Hindu symbols for mass mobilization but his politics was not purely communal — distinction from communalism

concepts.name: Bipin Chandra Pal: Revolutionary Thought and Spiritualized Nationalism
key_dimensions: Pal's concept of 'complete non-cooperation' — precursor to Gandhian ideas
Role of spirituality and Vedantic philosophy in his nationalism
Distinction between Pal's federalist vision of India and Tilak's Maharashtra-centric approach
UPSC trap: Pal is often conflated with Aurobindo Ghose — both Bengal-based but distinct ideologies

concepts.name: Lala Lajpat Rai: Punjab-Based Extremism and Social Reform
key_dimensions: Connection between Arya Samaj and his nationalist politics
Role in anti-partition agitation and labor movements in Punjab
His later writings on imperialism — 'Unhappy India' as a response to Katherine Mayo's 'Mother India'
UPSC trap: Lajpat Rai's deportation (1907) to Mandalay — often confused with Tilak's deportation/trial

concepts.name: The Partition of Bengal (1905) as Catalyst for Extremist Rise
key_dimensions: Curzon's administrative rationale vs. nationalist interpretation as divide-and-rule
How Partition shifted political power from Moderates to Extremists within Congress
Swadeshi and Boycott movements emerging directly from anti-partition agitation
UPSC trap: Partition of 1905 was annulled in 1911, but the 1947 partition of Bengal is entirely different — chronological conflation trap

concepts.name: Swadeshi Movement: Scope, Methods, and Limitations
key_dimensions: Economic dimension: boycott of Manchester cloth and Liverpool salt
Cultural dimension: national education, indigenous literature, and Bengali cultural renaissance
Social limitation: movement largely confined to upper-caste Hindus; Muslim peasantry alienation
UPSC trap: Swadeshi of 1905 was regionally concentrated (Bengal); contrast with Gandhi's all-India Swadeshi in Non-Cooperation

concepts.name: Boycott as a Political Weapon: Extremist Innovation
key_dimensions: Four-fold program of Extremists: Boycott, Swadeshi, National Education, Self-Government
Distinction between passive boycott (non-purchase) and active boycott (picketing) — government's legal response
Debate within Congress on extending boycott beyond Bengal to all-India level
UPSC trap: Boycott was NOT universally accepted by Moderates — key flashpoint at Calcutta Congress (1906) and Surat (1907)

concepts.name: Surat Split (1907): Causes, Events, and Consequences
key_dimensions: Immediate cause: dispute over presidency (Rash Behari Ghose vs. Tilak's preference) and adoption of Extremist resolutions
Role of Pherozeshah Mehta and Moderate tactics in engineering the split
Consequence: Congress captured by Moderates; Extremists effectively expelled until Lucknow 1916
UPSC trap: The Surat Split weakened the nationalist movement temporarily — often presented as straightforwardly negative, but it also forced ideological clarity

concepts.name: Tilak's Sedition Trials (1897 and 1908)
key_dimensions: 1897 trial: Tilak charged under Section 124-A IPC for articles in Kesari after Rand assassination
1908 trial: 6-year deportation to Mandalay — writings justifying Khudiram Bose's actions
Colonial legal strategy: use of sedition law to silence press and political dissent
UPSC trap: Section 124-A was drafted by Macaulay but NOT included in original 1860 IPC — added in 1870; Tilak's trials were landmark applications of this section

concepts.name: National Education Movement under Extremism
key_dimensions: Critique of Macaulay's education as creating 'clerks for Empire' — Extremist alternative vision
Establishment of National Council of Education in Bengal (1906) — key figures: Satish Chandra Mukherjee, Aurobindo
Bengal National College and Aurobindo Ghose's role as principal
UPSC trap: National Education Movement of 1906 is distinct from Wardha Scheme of Basic Education (1937) — both 'national education' but entirely different contexts

concepts.name: Aurobindo Ghose: Bridge Between Extremism and Revolutionary Nationalism
key_dimensions: Aurobindo's role in Extremist politics — editor of Yugantar and Karmayogin
Alipore Bomb Case (1908) and his eventual withdrawal from politics to Pondicherry
Concept of 'passive resistance' as articulated by Aurobindo — precursor to civil disobedience
UPSC trap: Aurobindo is associated with Extremists but is also a bridge to revolutionary terrorism — he is NOT classified as a revolutionary terrorist himself

concepts.name: Lucknow Pact (1916) and Extremist Re-entry into Congress
key_dimensions: Tilak's re-admission to Congress after 9-year exclusion — conditions and context
Role of Home Rule League agitation in rehabilitating Tilak's position
Significance of Congress-League Pact of Lucknow — Extremists' role in Hindu-Muslim unity
UPSC trap: Lucknow Pact is celebrated for Hindu-Muslim unity but also institutionalized separate electorates — a long-term negative consequence

concepts.name: Home Rule League Movement (1916): Tilak's vs. Annie Besant's League
key_dimensions: Tilak's Home Rule League (April 1916) vs. Annie Besant's (September 1916) — geographic divisions and organizational differences
Demand for Home Rule within the British Empire — distinction from complete independence
Government repression: Annie Besant's internment (1917) and its galvanizing effect
UPSC trap: Two separate Home Rule Leagues — UPSC frequently tests whether candidates can distinguish between them; Tilak's was first but Besant's was larger

concepts.name: Extremist Use of Press: Kesari, Mahratta, and Yugantar
key_dimensions: Tilak's Kesari (Marathi) and Mahratta (English) — different audiences, same nationalist message
Yugantar and Kal — Bengali revolutionary press associated with Extremist-to-revolutionary continuum
Colonial press laws used against Extremist papers: Seditious Meetings Act, Newspapers (Incitement to Offences) Act 1908
UPSC trap: Kesari is in Marathi, Mahratta in English — candidates often confuse the two; Tilak was tried for Kesari articles specifically

concepts.name: Bal-Pal-Lal and the Concept of 'Constructive Swadeshi'
key_dimensions: Beyond mere boycott — constructive programs: indigenous industries, national banks, national schools
Tilak's emphasis on self-sufficiency vs. Pal's spiritual-political synthesis vs. Lajpat Rai's social reform angle
How 'Constructive Swadeshi' anticipated Gandhi's constructive program of the 1920s-30s
UPSC trap: Extremists are often portrayed as purely destructive/agitational — their constructive program is underemphasized and frequently tested

concepts.name: Relationship Between Extremism and Early Revolutionary Terrorism
key_dimensions: Ideological overlap and distinction: Extremists sought mass agitation; revolutionaries sought armed action
Chaphekar brothers, Anushilan Samiti, Abhinav Bharat — organizational links to Extremist milieu
Government's deliberate conflation of Extremism with terrorism to justify repression
UPSC trap: Extremists and revolutionaries are distinct categories — Tilak publicly distanced himself from political violence even while being tried for incitement

concepts.name: Morley-Minto Reforms (1909) as Colonial Response to Extremist Challenge
key_dimensions: Reforms as a dual strategy: concession to Moderates + repression of Extremists
Introduction of separate electorates — British use of communalism to undermine unified nationalism
Why Extremists rejected the reforms: insufficient, designed to divide, no real self-government
UPSC trap: Morley explicitly said these reforms did NOT intend to introduce parliamentary democracy — statement frequently quoted in UPSC; Minto's role was administrative, Morley's ideological

concepts.name: Gender and Social Composition of the Extremist Movement
key_dimensions: Predominantly upper-caste Hindu male composition — limitation of mass base
Role of women in Swadeshi: picketing, making of Rakhi on Partition day — symbolic but not leadership roles
Muslim alienation from Extremist movement: Hindu symbolism as exclusionary factor leading to separate political identity
UPSC trap: The Swadeshi movement is celebrated as 'mass movement' but its social base was actually narrow — this is a key analytical distinction UPSC tests

concepts.name: Extremist Phase: Assessment of Achievements and Failures
key_dimensions: Achievement: expanded political discourse beyond petitions; introduced mass mobilization techniques
Achievement: Partition of Bengal annulled (1911) — validation of agitational politics
Failure: Surat Split weakened Congress; failure to build cross-religious, cross-caste coalitions
UPSC trap: Credit for annulment of Bengal Partition — was it Extremist agitation or Coronation Durbar political calculation by British? Both dimensions tested

concepts.name: Transition from Extremism to Gandhian Nationalism: Continuities and Breaks
key_dimensions: Continuities: mass mobilization, Swadeshi, non-cooperation, constructive program — all carried forward by Gandhi
Break: Gandhi's explicit non-violence vs. Extremists' ambiguity; Gandhi's cross-religious appeal vs. Hindu revivalist symbolism
Tilak-Gandhi relationship: Tilak supported Gandhi's early campaigns; Tilak's death (1920) coincided with Gandhi's rise
UPSC trap: Gandhi is often presented as a complete break from Extremism — the significant continuities are underappreciated and form the basis of analytical questions
